genres.name: The Vespa
genres.text: In April 1946 Piaggio presented a strange, rounded little vehicle at a golf club in Rome: the Vespa, Italian for wasp. The journalists did not quite know what to make of it. The scooter was cheap, clean and easy to ride, even in a smart suit. Fifteen years later the Vespa and its rival the Lambretta became the transport of the mods, decorated with mirrors and lamps.

genres.name: Existentialists at Le Tabou
genres.text: In April 1947 the club Le Tabou opened in a cellar on the Rue Dauphine, with permission to stay open until four in the morning. Boris Vian played trumpet there, Juliette Gréco sang and read poems, and Sartre and De Beauvoir dropped by. Young people in black polo necks and second-hand clothes called themselves existentialists. Newspapers made a craze of it, and within a few years the tourists came to look.
genres.listen: Si tu t'imagines is a poem by Raymond Queneau about a girl who thinks her youth will last for ever. Notice how Gréco speaks it more than sings it.

genres.name: The Empire Windrush at Tilbury
genres.text: On 22 June 1948 the Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury, with more than a thousand passengers from Jamaica and other Caribbean islands. On the quayside the calypso singer Lord Kitchener sang his song London Is the Place for Me for the Pathé camera. With these migrants came their music and their sound systems to England. Without them there would have been no ska in London, no rude boys and, later, no 2 Tone.
genres.listen: Kitchener only recorded the song in 1951. Hear how the calypso, with its horns and skipping rhythm, paints a cheerful picture of London, while the newcomers received a cold welcome there.

tracks.title: London Is the Place for Me

genres.name: The 45 rpm single
genres.text: On 31 March 1949 RCA Victor put the first 45 rpm singles in the shops: small, unbreakable seven-inch records with a big hole in the middle and one song per side. At first every kind of music had its own colour of vinyl, black for pop and orange for rhythm and blues. The single was cheap enough for pocket money. So teenagers got their own records, in their own rooms.

genres.name: The transfer of sovereignty to Indonesia

place.name: Amsterdam, Royal Palace on the Dam

genres.text: On 27 December 1949 Queen Juliana signed the transfer of sovereignty to Indonesia in the Royal Palace on the Dam. In the years that followed, hundreds of thousands of Indo-Dutch and Moluccans moved to the Netherlands. Among them were young musicians who had heard American rock 'n' roll, country, kroncong and Hawaiian music in the Indies. From that mixture, indorock grew in Dutch community centres and halls.

genres.name: Pleiners at the Leidseplein
genres.text: Around 1950 young artists and poets sat in the Amsterdam cafés Eijlders and Reynders near the Leidseplein. There the Vijftigers, among them Lucebert and Remco Campert, conspired together against the old poetry. The young people who hung around there were called pleiners. They wore black, listened to modern jazz and watched French films. They regularly fought with the dijkers of the Nieuwendijk.

genres.name: Rocket 88 in Sam Phillips's studio
genres.text: In March 1951 the band of the young Ike Turner recorded the song Rocket 88 in Sam Phillips's studio in Memphis, with Jackie Brenston as singer. Only Brenston's name was on the label. The guitar amplifier had broken on the way and therefore sounded raw and distorted. The song about a fast car went to number 1 in the rhythm and blues chart. Many experts call it the first rock 'n' roll record.
genres.listen: Hear the growling, distorted guitar under the pounding piano: a sound that came about by accident, because of a broken amplifier.

genres.name: The Catcher in the Rye
genres.text: On 16 July 1951 the publisher Little, Brown brought out the novel The Catcher in the Rye by J.D. Salinger. The narrator is Holden Caulfield, a teenager who has been expelled from school and thinks the adult world is full of phoneys. The book was meant for adults, but young people above all recognised themselves in it. Holden became the model of the lonely, awkward teenager, even before rock 'n' roll existed.

genres.name: The Moondog Coronation Ball
genres.text: On 21 March 1952 the disc jockey Alan Freed organised the Moondog Coronation Ball at the Cleveland Arena, a concert with Black rhythm and blues artists. Because of forged tickets and a printing error, about twice as many people came as the hall could hold. The police stopped the concert after a short time. It is regarded as the first big rock 'n' roll concert.
genres.listen: Hear the screaming saxophone of Paul Williams: this was the kind of dance music that Freed played on the radio for his young listeners.

genres.name: The Fred Perry shirt
genres.text: In 1952 the former tennis champion Fred Perry put a white tennis shirt of cotton piqué on the market, with short sleeves, a button placket and a laurel wreath as its logo. The first shirts were handed out to players at the Wimbledon tournament. A sports shirt, then, but it did not stay on the court. Mods later wore it buttoned up to the top, and skinheads after them. So a tennis shirt became a mark of youth cultures.

genres.name: The first British chart
genres.text: On 14 November 1952 the music paper New Musical Express printed the first British chart. Its founder Percy Dickins phoned about twenty record shops himself and counted by hand which records sold best. At number 1 was Al Martino with Here in My Heart. From then on anyone could see every week what was popular, and fans wanted to see their favourite climb.
genres.listen: Hear the big, soaring voice of Al Martino with a full orchestra: this is how a hit sounded just before rock 'n' roll arrived.

genres.name: The Moka Bar in Soho
genres.text: In 1953 the Moka Bar opened at 29 Frith Street in the London district of Soho, with a gleaming espresso machine from the Italian brand Gaggia. According to the stories, more than a thousand cups of coffee a day soon passed over the counter. After the Moka, coffee bars appeared all over London. There young people could hang around for hours without alcohol, and some had a jukebox or a live band.

genres.name: The Teddy Boys
genres.text: On 23 September 1953 the Daily Express wrote about a group of boys who called themselves Edwardians and shortened it to Teddy Boys. Working-class boys from South London wore long jackets with velvet collars, narrow trousers, thin ties and thick-soled shoes, with their hair in a greasy quiff. They spent their own wages on made-to-measure clothes. When rock 'n' roll came over from America, they became its first fans.
genres.listen: See You Later, Alligator was a big British hit in 1956 for Bill Haley, the hero of the Teds. Count how often the chorus comes back: it was made for shouting along in the hall.

genres.name: Marlon Brando in The Wild One
genres.text: In The Wild One Marlon Brando played Johnny, the leader of a motorcycle gang that throws a small town into turmoil, in a leather jacket and cap. Asked what he is rebelling against, he answers drily: what have you got? The British film censors thought the film so dangerous for the young that it stayed banned until 1967. Even so, Brando's leather jacket became the uniform of the rockers.

genres.name: The Regency TR-1, the first transistor radio
genres.text: On 18 October 1954 the company I.D.E.A. of Indianapolis announced the Regency TR-1 together with Texas Instruments, the first transistor radio for ordinary consumers. It fitted in a coat pocket and cost 49.95 dollars. More than a hundred thousand were sold. With a gadget like that, a teenager could listen to his own station in the street, on the beach or under the covers, out of his parents' reach.

genres.name: Bill Haley: Rock Around the Clock
genres.text: Bill Haley & His Comets recorded Rock Around the Clock in 1954, but it only became a hit when the song played under the opening titles of the film Blackboard Jungle from 25 March 1955. Young people went to the cinema to hear the tune. In July it was number 1 in America, the first rock 'n' roll record ever to get there. Adults saw it as proof that rock 'n' roll was dangerous.
genres.listen: Count the bars of a verse: it is a twelve-bar blues. Notice too the double-slapped double bass and the little drum roll at the start.

genres.name: Nozems and dijkers
genres.text: In the 1950s Dutch young people also got a group of their own: the nozems. They wore jeans and leather jackets, combed their hair into a greasy quiff and hung around on their mopeds at the snack bar. In Amsterdam the roughest were called dijkers, after the Nieuwendijk where they met. Adults saw them as problem youth. Nobody knows exactly where the word nozem comes from.

genres.name: James Dean in Rebel Without a Cause
genres.text: Rebel Without a Cause played in American cinemas from 27 October 1955, almost a month after James Dean was killed in a car accident on 30 September, aged 24. He plays Jim Stark, a teenager who feels misunderstood by his parents. His red jacket, white T-shirt and jeans became a uniform. Because of his early death, Dean remained the young rebel for ever.

genres.name: Mary Quant opens Bazaar
genres.text: In November 1955 the young designer Mary Quant and her husband Alexander Plunket Greene opened the shop Bazaar on King's Road in Chelsea. She sold clothes she wanted to wear herself: short dresses, bright tights and simple shapes. In the 1960s she became known for the miniskirt, although Quant herself said the girls of King's Road had invented it. Her shop windows became a catwalk.

genres.name: Elvis Presley: Heartbreak Hotel
genres.text: Heartbreak Hotel was Elvis Presley's first single for RCA and came out on 27 January 1956. It became his first number 1 in America and in a few months made him the biggest idol of the teenagers. The recording in Nashville sounds hollow with echo. For Teddy Boys, nozems and rockers, Elvis, with his quiff and hip movements, was the example.
genres.listen: Listen to the empty space around the voice. Elvis sings almost in a whisper, the band plays softly, and yet it sounds more exciting than much louder rock.

genres.name: The 2i's Coffee Bar
genres.text: In April 1956 two wrestlers opened the 2i's Coffee Bar in Old Compton Street in Soho. In the small cellar, skiffle and rock 'n' roll groups played for teenagers with a cup of espresso. There Tommy Hicks was discovered, who as Tommy Steele became the first British rock 'n' roll star. Cliff Richard and Hank Marvin also started there. It became the nursery of British rock.
genres.listen: Rock with the Caveman from 1956 was Tommy Steele's first hit. Does it sound like real rock 'n' roll, or can you hear that the British still had to learn it?

genres.name: Gene Vincent: Be-Bop-A-Lula
genres.text: On 4 May 1956 Gene Vincent and his band The Blue Caps recorded Be-Bop-A-Lula in Owen Bradley's studio in Nashville. Capitol released it in June, first as the B-side, but DJs preferred to play this song. It reached the top ten in America. In England Vincent became a hero of the rockers, and he later performed there in black leather.
genres.listen: Hear the slapback echo on the voice: a short repeat right after each word. Notice too the fast guitar solo by Cliff Gallup.

genres.name: Riots at Rock Around the Clock
genres.text: In September 1956 the film Rock Around the Clock with Bill Haley came to British cinemas. At the Trocadero at Elephant and Castle, Teddy Boys slashed the seats, and when the police tried to drive off dancing teenagers, bottles and fireworks flew. Things also went wrong in Manchester, and Birmingham, Blackpool and Belfast banned the film. The newspapers had their proof: rock 'n' roll was dangerous.

genres.name: John Stephen in Carnaby Street
genres.text: In 1957, after a fire at his first shop, the young Scot John Stephen opened the shop His Clothes in Carnaby Street, then still a quiet back street. He sold colourful, tight-fitting menswear to boys with a wage packet, with loud music and shop assistants of their own age. By 1967 he had fifteen shops in the street and was called the king of Carnaby Street.
genres.listen: In Dedicated Follower of Fashion from 1966, The Kinks poke fun at the fashionable boys of Carnaby Street. Hear the music-hall style of the chorus, almost an old English drinking song.

genres.name: American Bandstand
genres.text: On 5 August 1957 the dance programme from Philadelphia went out nationwide on ABC, as American Bandstand, presented by Dick Clark. Every afternoon teenagers from the neighbourhood danced in the studio to the latest records, and all over America their contemporaries watched after school. What was played on Bandstand became a hit. At the Hop by Danny & the Juniors was one of them.
genres.listen: At the Hop names the dances of the moment. Hear how the song is an invitation to join in, exactly what a TV dance programme wanted.

genres.name: Beatniks in North Beach
genres.text: In September 1957 On the Road by Jack Kerouac appeared, a novel about restless journeys through America, written to the rhythm of bebop. The book became the handbook of the Beat Generation. On 2 April 1958 the columnist Herb Caen in San Francisco used the mocking word beatnik, partly after the Russian Sputnik. Beards, polo necks, poetry and jazz in coffee houses in North Beach became a recognisable style.
genres.listen: Kerouac read his prose aloud while Steve Allen improvised on the piano. Hear how he lets his sentences run like a jazz solo.

genres.name: Rockers and ton-up boys
genres.text: In the late 1950s young motorcyclists gathered at the Ace Cafe on the North Circular Road in London. They were called ton-up boys, after the hundred miles an hour they wanted to reach. A well-known game was record racing: coin in the jukebox, run to the motorbike and be back before the record had finished. In the 1960s they were called rockers, after their music.
genres.listen: Shakin' All Over by Johnny Kidd & The Pirates was in 1960 one of the few British rock songs that the rockers took seriously. Listen to the trembling, low-tuned guitar riff.

genres.name: The Tielman Brothers at Expo 58
genres.text: The Tielman Brothers came from Indonesia to Breda in 1956. In 1958 they were allowed to stand in for a quarter of an hour in the Dutch pavilion at the world exhibition in Brussels, during the break of a Hawaiian band. They played much longer, threw their guitars to each other and played bass with their teeth. The first Dutch rock 'n' roll single followed, and gigs in German clubs, such as on the Reeperbahn.
genres.listen: Listen to the fast runs on Andy Tielman's guitar. Can you hear the Hawaiian influence in the sliding notes?

genres.name: The Notting Hill riots
genres.text: At the end of August 1958 groups of white youths, among them many Teddy Boys, attacked West Indian residents of Notting Hill for a week, with iron bars, knives and petrol bombs. Black youths defended themselves. Some one hundred and forty people were arrested. In response, Claudia Jones organised a Caribbean carnival in a hall in St Pancras in January 1959. The Notting Hill Carnival later grew out of it.

genres.name: Oh Boy! and Move It
genres.text: The producer Jack Good wanted a fast TV programme with music only. At ITV he got Oh Boy!, and the series began on 13 September 1958. In the first episode the seventeen-year-old Cliff Richard sang Move It, at Good's insistence and not his intended A-side. Move It is regarded as the first real British rock 'n' roll record. Cliff curled his lip like Elvis and the girls in the hall screamed.
genres.listen: Listen to the guitar intro by Ernie Shear. Can you hear that the British could now play a solid rock riff themselves?

genres.name: Eddie Cochran: C'mon Everybody
genres.text: Eddie Cochran was a skilled musician who often played guitar and bass himself in the studio. C'mon Everybody came out in October 1958 and is about a party while the parents are away. After Summertime Blues, about a teenager who has to work and cannot get time off, it was his second teenage song. In England Cochran was even more popular than at home.
genres.listen: The song is built on a stop-time riff: the band plays a short motif and then falls silent, and in that silence Cochran sings his line. That gives the voice all the attention.

genres.name: Cliff Richard: Living Doll
genres.text: Living Doll, written by Lionel Bart for the film Serious Charge, came out on 10 July 1959. Cliff Richard and his band The Drifters played it as a quiet, acoustic shuffle. It became his first number 1 in England and sold more than a million copies. The wild British Elvis of a year earlier had become a nice boy whom mothers could appreciate too.
genres.listen: Compare Living Doll with Move It from 1958. Can you hear the influence of country in the skipping rhythm and the soft singing?

genres.name: Miles Davis: Kind of Blue
genres.text: On 17 August 1959 Kind of Blue by Miles Davis came out, recorded in two sessions with, among others, John Coltrane and the pianist Bill Evans. Instead of fast chord changes as in bebop, Davis used a few scales over which the soloists could play freely. For arty types, beatniks and the first mods, the modernists, this was the soundtrack: music to listen to, not to dance to.
genres.listen: In So What the bass asks the question and piano and horns answer with two chords. Compare it with Be-Bop by Milt Jackson and Coltrane: there the chords fly past.

genres.name: Alan Freed and the payola scandal
genres.text: The DJ Alan Freed had made the term rock 'n' roll popular and was one of the first to play Black rhythm and blues for a white audience. On 21 November 1959 the station WABC fired him, because he refused to declare that he had never taken money to play records. That is called payola. In 1960 Dick Clark also had to testify, but he got off lightly. Freed's career was over.

genres.name: À bout de souffle and the nouvelle vague
genres.text: On 16 March 1960 À bout de souffle by Jean-Luc Godard had its premiere in Paris, a film with a small budget, a loose handheld camera and jumps in the editing. For the arty crowd in Paris and on the Leidseplein, the nouvelle vague was their own cinema. Two years earlier Louis Malle had already shown how well jazz suited such films: Miles Davis improvised the music for Ascenseur pour l'échafaud.
genres.listen: Miles Davis played the music for Ascenseur pour l'échafaud in December 1957 in a single night session, watching the images. Hear how little he needs: a few chords, a lot of space and a muted trumpet.

genres.name: The Dr. Martens 1460
genres.text: On 1 April 1960 the shoe factory Griggs in the English village of Wollaston made the first Dr. Martens boot with eight eyelets. The model number 1460 comes from that date. The cushioned sole had been devised by the German doctor Klaus Märtens, and Griggs added the yellow stitching. At first postmen and factory workers wore the boot. Later it became the shoe of skinheads, punks and 2 Tone fans.

genres.name: Radio Veronica
genres.text: In April 1960 the first test broadcast of Radio Veronica began from an old German lightship off the coast of Scheveningen. Because the ship lay outside Dutch waters, the rules of the broadcasting organisations did not apply. Veronica played pop music and charts all day, something public radio hardly did. For Dutch teenagers the pirate station became their own radio station.

genres.name: The death of Eddie Cochran
genres.text: In April 1960 Eddie Cochran and Gene Vincent were on tour together in England. After a concert in Bristol they took a taxi to London on the night of 16 April. Near Chippenham the driver lost control of the wheel. Cochran was thrown from the car and died the next day, aged 21. Vincent was injured. For the British rockers Cochran became a hero.
genres.listen: Three Steps to Heaven was Cochran's new single when he died. Soon afterwards it was number 1 in England. How does this cheerful love song sound when you know what happened?

genres.name: The Beatles in Hamburg
genres.text: On 17 August 1960 The Beatles played their first night at the Indra, a small club in the Hamburg entertainment district of St. Pauli. The five boys from Liverpool had to play for hours every night for sailors, tourists and German young people. After complaints about the noise they moved to the Kaiserkeller in October. In Hamburg they became a tight band, and there they went on stage in black leather jackets.
genres.listen: In this instrumental, hear the two guitars playing the melody together: The Beatles recorded it in Hamburg in 1961, in the style of The Shadows.

genres.name: The Blue Diamonds: Ramona
genres.text: The brothers Riem and Ruud de Wolff came as children from Batavia to Driebergen. As The Blue Diamonds they sang in two-part harmony, like the Everly Brothers. Their fast version of Ramona, a song from 1928, was number 1 in the Netherlands in October 1960 and at the end of the year in West Germany too. Indopop sounded softer and more polished than the wild shows of the Tielmans.
genres.listen: Listen to the two voices moving right next to each other. Compare it with the guitar show of the Tielman Brothers: which music would a mother rather hear?

genres.name: The twist at the Peppermint Lounge
genres.text: In October 1961 rich New Yorkers discovered the Peppermint Lounge, a small bar near Times Square. Joey Dee and the Starliters played there and everyone danced the twist: you swivel your hips back and forth without holding your partner. After gossip magazines had spotted celebrities on the dance floor, adults wanted to twist too. The song Peppermint Twist was number 1 in America for three weeks in January 1962.
genres.listen: Hear the fast, rousing saxophone and the shouted words: the band played this every night for a packed dance floor.

genres.name: Mods in Stamford Hill
genres.text: In September 1962 the magazine Town ran a report on boys from Stamford Hill who lived for clothes and fun. The photographer Don McCullin portrayed, among others, the fifteen-year-old Mark Feld, the later Marc Bolan. These mods, short for modernists, wore made-to-measure suits and rode Italian scooters with a parka over the suit. They danced to soul, rhythm and blues and ska in clubs such as The Flamingo.
genres.listen: Green Onions by Booker T. & the M.G.'s was a fixture in the mod clubs. Hear how the Hammond organ and the sharp guitar alternate over a tight blues.

genres.name: Ready Steady Go!
genres.text: On 9 August 1963 Ready Steady Go! began on British TV, every Friday evening, with the slogan that the weekend starts here. Bands played live among dancing young people in the studio, and the presenter Cathy McGowan had answered an advertisement seeking a typical teenager as an adviser. What she and the dancers wore, the mods wore a week later. In this way the mod style spread across the country.
genres.listen: 5-4-3-2-1 by Manfred Mann became the theme tune. Whatcha Gonna Do About It by the Small Faces shows how a real mod band sounded.

genres.name: Top of the Pops
genres.text: On 1 January 1964 the BBC broadcast the first Top of the Pops from a studio in a former church in Manchester, presented by Jimmy Savile. Dusty Springfield opened with I Only Want to Be with You, followed by the Rolling Stones. Every week millions of teenagers saw the hits of the moment. For more than forty years the programme determined what a British idol was.
genres.listen: In I Only Want to Be with You, hear the full, Motown-like production. Dusty Springfield brought American soul to a British audience.

tracks.title: I Only Want to Be with You

genres.name: Millie Small: My Boy Lollipop
genres.text: Chris Blackwell of Island Records brought the Jamaican teenager Millie Small to London. The guitarist Ernest Ranglin turned My Boy Lollipop into a ska song. The single came out in early 1964 and reached number 2 in England. It was the first Jamaican record to sell millions of copies worldwide. Ska could now be heard outside the West Indian neighbourhoods too, and the mods danced to it.
genres.listen: Listen to the guitar that keeps striking between the beats: the offbeat of ska. Above it Small sings high and exuberant, almost like a child.

genres.name: Radio Caroline
genres.text: On Easter Saturday, 28 March 1964, Radio Caroline began broadcasting from an old Danish ferry off the English east coast. The Irish businessman Ronan O'Rahilly had been unable to get airtime for the records of his artist Georgie Fame. The first record played was probably Not Fade Away by the Rolling Stones. The BBC played little pop, so British teenagers tuned in to the pirates in large numbers.

genres.name: Mods and rockers in Brighton
genres.text: At Easter 1964 there were fights between mods and rockers in Clacton. At Whitsun, on 18 and 19 May, things went wrong again in Margate and Brighton, where mods attacked a small group of rockers on the beach. The newspapers wrote of an invasion of scum. The sociologist Stanley Cohen later showed that the reporting made the groups bigger and better known than they were.
genres.listen: In 1973 The Who made the rock opera Quadrophenia about it, filmed in 1979. In 5:15, hear how the band sends the train to Brighton thundering along.

genres.name: The Rolling Stones at the Kurhaus
genres.text: On 8 August 1964 the Rolling Stones played their first Dutch concert, at the stylish Kurhaus in Scheveningen. After a few minutes a fight broke out, young people climbed on to the stage and the police cut the power. According to Bill Wyman the band was on stage for only seven minutes. Then the audience wrecked the hall: chairs were torn loose and thrown into the chandeliers.
genres.listen: It's All Over Now was in the summer of 1964 the Stones' first number 1 in England. Hear the twelve-string guitar and the sloppy, excited playing together.

genres.name: Biba
genres.text: Barbara Hulanicki and her husband Stephen Fitz-Simon started with mail-order clothing. In May 1964 they sold thousands of pink gingham dresses through the Daily Mirror. In September that year they opened the first Biba shop in an old chemist's on Abingdon Road in Kensington. With dark colours, feather boas and low prices, Biba became the place where girls on an office salary bought their own Swinging London.

genres.name: Provo
genres.text: In May 1965 Roel van Duijn announced the birth of Provo with pamphlets, together with Rob Stolk and the anti-smoking magician Robert Jasper Grootveld. From late July there were happenings every Saturday evening at the Lieverdje on the Spui, a statue that a cigarette manufacturer had donated to the city. Provo wanted to provoke the middle classes and came up with white plans, such as free white bicycles for everyone.

genres.name: Hippies in Haight-Ashbury
genres.text: On 5 September 1965 the journalist Michael Fallon wrote in the San Francisco Examiner about young people in the Haight-Ashbury district and called them hippies. The word stuck. The hippies were against the war in Vietnam and against their parents' materialism. They wore long hair, beads and home-made clothes, experimented with LSD and listened to bands such as the Grateful Dead and Jefferson Airplane.
genres.listen: Jefferson Airplane came from San Francisco. In Somebody to Love, listen to the singing of Grace Slick, which rises like a siren above the guitars.

genres.name: Hitweek and nederbeat
genres.text: In September 1965 the first issue of Hitweek appeared, founded by Willem de Ridder and Peter Muller. The magazine wrote about pop music, fashion and the underground, and had ties with Provo. It appeared just when the Netherlands was getting its own beat groups, nederbeat. The Outsiders from Amsterdam and Q65 from The Hague played raw rhythm and blues in English, with hits in the Dutch charts.
genres.listen: Listen to The Life I Live by Q65 and Lying All the Time by The Outsiders. How do they sound compared with the Rolling Stones and The Who?

genres.name: The Who: My Generation
genres.text: My Generation by The Who came out on 29 October 1965 and reached number 2 in England. Roger Daltrey sings that he hopes to die before he gets old. It became the anthem of the mods and one of the best-known songs about the generation gap. The bassist John Entwistle plays short solos, and at the end Pete Townshend lets his guitar ring around in the amplifier.
genres.listen: Hear how Daltrey stutters, as if he is too angry to get his words out. Count the key changes: the song goes up a tone three times.

genres.name: Boudewijn de Groot: Welterusten mijnheer de president
genres.text: On 26 February 1966 Welterusten mijnheer de president by Boudewijn de Groot came out, with words by Lennaert Nijgh. It is a polite, biting lullaby for the American president Johnson, in which the singer asks how he can sleep while fighting goes on in Vietnam. It was one of the first Dutch-language songs against that war. From then on De Groot was called a protest singer, a label he was not happy with.
genres.listen: Notice the contrast between the soft, almost sweet melody and the harsh content of the words. Why does that combination work so well?

genres.name: Twiggy, the face of 1966
genres.text: On 23 February 1966 the newspaper Daily Express called the sixteen-year-old Lesley Hornby from London the face of 1966. A hairdresser in Mayfair had cut her hair very short a few weeks earlier, and the photographs of it stood out. Under the name Twiggy she became the best-known model of the 1960s, with her big eyes, long eyelashes and miniskirt. Her boyish look was copied by girls everywhere.

genres.name: Smoke bombs at the royal wedding
genres.text: On 10 March 1966 Princess Beatrix married the German diplomat Claus von Amsberg in Amsterdam. Provo had proclaimed the day a day of anarchy. As the golden coach drove through the Raadhuisstraat, Provos threw smoke bombs and the procession was engulfed in white clouds. More than two million Dutch people watched it live on TV. The police hit back hard, which only made Provo more popular.

genres.name: UFO Club
genres.text: On 23 December 1966 Joe Boyd and John Hopkins opened the UFO Club in an Irish dance hall under a cinema on Tottenham Court Road. On Friday nights there were light shows, experimental films, poetry and long improvisations. Pink Floyd was the first house band, then Soft Machine. It was the London centre of the psychedelic underground, until the club had to move to the Roundhouse half a year later.
genres.listen: Interstellar Overdrive lasts almost ten minutes. Hear how Pink Floyd, after a short riff, let go of the fixed form and start experimenting with sound.

genres.name: The Human Be-In
genres.text: On 14 January 1967 twenty to thirty thousand people came to the Polo Fields in Golden Gate Park for the Human Be-In. The occasion was the new ban on LSD in California. The Grateful Dead and Jefferson Airplane played, poets such as Allen Ginsberg read aloud, and Timothy Leary called on people to turn on, tune in and drop out. The Be-In was the starting signal for the Summer of Love.
genres.listen: White Rabbit by Jefferson Airplane builds like a bolero, louder and louder, until Grace Slick calls out the last line. What do you think it is about?

genres.name: Scott McKenzie: San Francisco
genres.text: John Phillips of The Mamas & the Papas wrote San Francisco (Be Sure to Wear Flowers in Your Hair) to announce the Monterey Pop Festival. His friend Scott McKenzie sang it and the single came out on 13 May 1967. It became a worldwide hit and called on young people to come to San Francisco with flowers in their hair. That summer tens of thousands came.
genres.listen: Notice how soft and friendly everything sounds: acoustic guitar, a warm voice, not a trace of protest. This is the brochure of the Summer of Love.

tracks.title: San Francisco (Be Sure to Wear Flowers in Your Hair)

genres.name: Monterey Pop Festival
genres.text: From 16 to 18 June 1967 the first big pop festival was held in Monterey, California. Otis Redding won over a white hippie audience there. On the last evening Jimi Hendrix, already a star in England but still unknown at home, ended his performance with Wild Thing. Then he knelt by his guitar, poured lighter fluid over it and set it on fire.
genres.listen: In Wild Thing, hear how Hendrix plays with feedback and the tremolo of his guitar. Compare it with Try a Little Tenderness by Otis, which gets faster and more intense all the time.

tracks.title: Try a Little Tenderness (live in Monterey)

genres.name: Rude boys in Kingston
genres.text: After Jamaica's independence in 1962 many young men moved to Kingston, where there was no work for them. Some became rude boys, with tight suits, pork-pie hats and a reputation for violence. Singers took sides. In 1967 Desmond Dekker sang in 007 (Shanty Town) about rudies who start riots, and Dandy Livingstone urged them to stop in Rudy, a Message to You.
genres.listen: Both songs are rocksteady: slower than ska, with a heavy bass. In Rudy, hear the trombone of Rico Rodriguez, who twelve years later also played on the version by The Specials.

genres.name: Paradiso
genres.text: In October 1967 hippies led by Willem de Ridder occupied an old church on the Weteringschans. On 30 March 1968 the Cosmic Relaxation Center Paradiso opened there, with some thirteen hundred visitors, a folk-rock band and a steel band from Suriname. Less than two months later Pink Floyd played there. Paradiso became the place where Dutch young people could see the newest British and American bands.

genres.name: Desmond Dekker: Israelites
genres.text: Desmond Dekker released Israelites in Jamaica in 1968. In April 1969 it was number 1 in England, the first Jamaican record ever to get there, and also in the Netherlands and West Germany. Dekker sings about a man who works from early morning to late at night and still has no money. The new skinheads made the song their own.
genres.listen: Listen to the slow, springy rhythm of early reggae. Can you understand what Dekker sings? Many British fans could not, and sang their own words to it.

genres.name: The first skinheads
genres.text: Around 1968 the hard mods from the English working-class districts were called skinheads. They cut their hair very short and wore jeans, braces, Ben Sherman shirts and Dr. Martens. They had nothing to do with the far right then: they danced to ska and early reggae by Jamaican artists. In 1969 the London band Symarip even recorded a song with the title Skinhead Moonstomp.
genres.listen: Skinhead Moonstomp is an adaptation of Moon Hop by Derrick Morgan. Hear the little organ on the offbeat and the voice that addresses the dancers.

genres.name: Woodstock
genres.text: From 15 to 18 August 1969 about four hundred thousand people came to Max Yasgur's farm in Bethel, while the organisers had counted on fifty thousand. It rained, there was too little food and the roads were jammed. Even so, it stayed peaceful. Richie Havens opened, and Jimi Hendrix closed on Monday morning for a much smaller audience. The festival became the symbol of a generation.
genres.listen: Richie Havens had to play longer and longer because other bands were stuck in traffic. He improvised Freedom on the spot. With Hendrix the American national anthem sounds like bombs and sirens.

genres.name: Altamont
genres.text: On 6 December 1969 the Rolling Stones gave a free concert at the Altamont racetrack in California, for about three hundred thousand people. Security was in the hands of the Hells Angels, paid in beer. During Under My Thumb one of them stabbed the eighteen-year-old Meredith Hunter to death, after he had drawn a revolver. Four people died that day. For many, the dream of Woodstock was over.
genres.listen: Gimme Shelter came out a few days later on Let It Bleed. Hear how Merry Clayton screams the line about rape and murder until her voice breaks.

genres.name: The Loft and Love Saves the Day
genres.text: On 14 February 1970 David Mancuso held a party titled Love Saves the Day in his home on Broadway in New York. Some one hundred guests came. It became a regular private party on Saturday nights, by invitation only, where Black, Latino and gay young people danced together. Mancuso played the records without mixing them, on an exceptionally good sound system. This is where disco began.
genres.listen: Soul Makossa by the Cameroonian Manu Dibango was discovered at the Loft and then played everywhere. Hear how the saxophone and the repeated call build a groove that does not need to go anywhere.

genres.name: Joni Mitchell: Woodstock
genres.text: Joni Mitchell wrote Woodstock about the festival while she was not there herself. She was in a hotel room in New York and followed the news on TV. Her friend Graham Nash told her about it. Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young made a hard rock version of it in March 1970. Matthews Southern Comfort recorded it quietly and softly and with it reached number 1 in England in October 1970.
genres.listen: Compare the two versions. How does the mood of the same song change through tempo, instruments and singing?

genres.name: Joni Mitchell: Big Yellow Taxi
genres.text: Big Yellow Taxi is on Ladies of the Canyon, Joni Mitchell's album from April 1970. She wrote it in Hawaii, when she saw green mountains from her hotel window and a big car park below. It is one of the first pop songs about the environment. Mitchell often tuned her guitar to an open tuning, which gave her chords that are hard to play on an ordinary guitar.
genres.listen: The words are gloomy, but the song sounds cheerful, with a skipping guitar and a little laugh at the end. Why would Mitchell choose that contrast?

genres.name: Northern soul
genres.text: In his record shop Soul City in London, Dave Godin noticed that football fans from the north only wanted fast, stomping soul records from the 1960s. He gave them a bin of their own: northern soul. In June 1970 he used the term for the first time in his column in Blues & Soul. In clubs in Manchester and Wigan young people danced all night to obscure American singles.
genres.listen: Tainted Love by Gloria Jones from 1964 flopped in America but became a northern soul classic. Compare it with the well-known version by Soft Cell from 1981.

genres.name: Holland Pop Festival at Kralingen
genres.text: From 26 to 28 June 1970 the Holland Pop Festival was held in the Kralingse Bos in Rotterdam, the first big multi-day pop festival on the European continent. Pink Floyd, Jefferson Airplane, Santana, The Byrds and Canned Heat, among others, played. About 35,000 people bought a ticket, but almost a hundred thousand came, over the fences or in boats across the Kralingse Plas.
genres.listen: Going Up the Country by Canned Heat, with a flute like a little bird, was also a favourite song of Woodstock. Hear how the longing for the countryside sounds.

genres.name: The Melkweg
genres.text: On 17 July 1970 a group of friends organised a gig by Groep 1850 in an empty dairy factory on the Lijnbaansgracht, close to the Leidseplein. That is how the Melkweg began. In the first years it was only open in summer, with a café, a restaurant and a hall for music and theatre. Together with Paradiso, the Melkweg made Amsterdam a magnet for young travellers from all over Europe.

genres.name: The Dam sleepers
genres.text: In the summer of 1970 six hundred to a thousand young travellers and hippies slept every night on the Dam, around the National Monument. Residents and shopkeepers complained. When a ban on sleeping came into force on 24 August, it led to riots with the police. A day later sailors and marines, on their own initiative, marched on to the Dam with belts and chased the young people away. The government disapproved of the action.

genres.name: Glitter on Top of the Pops
genres.text: In March 1971 Marc Bolan of T. Rex appeared on Top of the Pops with glitter on his cheeks. The idea came from Chelita Secunda, who worked with T. Rex. Hot Love was number 1 at the time. That glitter is often seen as the beginning of glam rock. From then on boys and girls came to the concerts of Bolan, Bowie and Slade in platform shoes, satin and make-up.
genres.listen: Hot Love is really a simple boogie with a long singalong coda. Hear how little is needed: three chords, handclaps and a little chorus.

genres.name: David Bowie: Starman and Ziggy Stardust
genres.text: On 16 June 1972 The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars came out, an album about a rock star from space. On 6 July David Bowie sang Starman on Top of the Pops, with dyed red hair, and casually put an arm around the guitarist Mick Ronson. For many British teenagers that evening it was a revelation. They saw that you were allowed to be different.
genres.listen: In the chorus of Starman the melody jumps up an octave on the word star. The same little jump is in Over the Rainbow. Can you hear it?

genres.name: Kool Herc in the Bronx
genres.text: On 11 August 1973 the eighteen-year-old Clive Campbell, DJ Kool Herc, played at his sister Cindy's party in the recreation room at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in the Bronx. Herc came from Jamaica and knew the sound systems. He noticed that dancers let go most at the drum break of funk records, and stretched that part out with two copies of the same record. That party is regarded as the beginning of hip hop.
genres.listen: Apache by the Incredible Bongo Band was one of Herc's favourite breaks. Listen to the drum and bongo part: Herc played that part again and again.

tracks.title: Give It Up or Turnit a Loose

genres.name: Wigan Casino
genres.text: In the early morning of 23 September 1973 the Wigan Casino held its first all-nighter, with DJ Russ Winstanley. Until 1981 thousands of young people danced all night every week to fast soul, with spins, flips and talcum powder on the floor. The evening always ended with the same three songs, the three before eight. More than four million visitors came in eight years.
genres.listen: I'm on My Way by Dean Parrish and Time Will Pass You By by Tobi Legend belong to those three closing songs. Can you feel how the tempo keeps the dancers awake to the end?

genres.name: CBGB
genres.text: In December 1973 Hilly Kristal opened the club CBGB on the Bowery in New York, for country, bluegrass and blues. That music hardly ever came. In 1974 Television and the Ramones got a regular spot there, and on 16 August the Ramones played to an almost empty room. Patti Smith, Blondie and Talking Heads followed. CBGB became the home of New York punk.
genres.listen: Marquee Moon by Television lasts ten minutes, with long guitar lines that weave through each other. Not all punk was short and fast.

genres.name: 430 King's Road: from Let It Rock to SEX
genres.text: In 1971 Malcolm McLaren and Vivienne Westwood took over a shop at 430 King's Road. At first it was called Let It Rock and they sold clothes and records for Teddy Boys. In 1974 it became SEX, with rubber, leather, bondage clothing and provocative T-shirts. Around the shop formed the group of young people from which the Sex Pistols emerged. In December 1976 the shop was called Seditionaries.

genres.name: The Rocky Horror Picture Show
genres.text: On 14 August 1975 the film The Rocky Horror Picture Show had its premiere in London, a creepy musical full of glitter, rock 'n' roll and dressing up. At first the film was no success. From 1976 a cinema in New York showed it at midnight, and there the audience began to come in costume, dance along and shout at the screen. So a film grew into a party for young people who felt different.
genres.listen: Hear how the song explains the dance steps, so that the hall can join in: exactly what the audience did at the midnight screenings.

tracks.artist: Little Nell, Patricia Quinn, Richard O'Brien & The Rocky Horror Picture Show
tracks.title: The Time Warp

genres.name: The first gig of the Sex Pistols

place.name: London, St Martin's School of Art, Charing Cross Road

genres.text: On 6 November 1975 the Sex Pistols played their first gig, in the canteen of St Martin's art school in London. The bassist Glen Matlock studied there. They were the support act for the band Bazooka Joe, and borrowed its amplifiers and drum kit. After about twenty minutes Bazooka Joe pulled the plug. Only a few dozen people watched, but a year later punk was in the news everywhere.
genres.listen: The Pistols played this song by The Who that evening. Hear the fiercely chopped chords and the angry words about someone who feels replaced.

genres.name: Suriname becomes independent
genres.text: On 25 November 1975 Suriname became an independent country. In the months before and after, tens of thousands of Surinamese left for the Netherlands, in 1975 alone about forty thousand. Many of them ended up in Amsterdam, among other places in the new flats of the Bijlmer. They brought their own music, food and language. So Surinamese music, such as kaseko, also became part of Dutch nightlife.

genres.name: Ramones
genres.text: On 23 April 1976 the first album by the Ramones came out, four boys from Queens in leather jackets and ripped jeans who all took the surname Ramone. Fourteen songs in less than thirty minutes, almost without guitar solos. In July they played in London at the Roundhouse. In the audience stood young people who soon afterwards started a band or a fanzine themselves.
genres.listen: Listen to Johnny Ramone's guitar: only power chords, struck hard, without a pause. Count how often the drummer Tommy lets the tempo drop for a moment: never.

genres.name: Sniffin' Glue
genres.text: On 4 July 1976 the bank clerk Mark Perry from Deptford saw the Ramones at the Roundhouse. A week later, on 13 July, he made the first issue of Sniffin' Glue, named after a Ramones song. He typed it on a child's typewriter, wrote headlines with a felt-tip pen and photocopied fifty copies. It became the example for hundreds of fanzines: anyone could write about music.
genres.listen: Now I Wanna Sniff Some Glue lasts less than two minutes. The title is a joke about boredom. How seriously should you take punk lyrics?

tracks.title: Now I Wanna Sniff Some Glue

genres.name: Stiff Records
genres.text: Dave Robinson and Jake Riviera started the independent label Stiff Records in 1976 with a loan of four hundred pounds. The first single, So It Goes by Nick Lowe, came out on 14 August 1976. On 22 October New Rose by The Damned followed, seen by many as the first British punk single. Small labels such as Stiff and Rough Trade made records outside the big companies.
genres.listen: New Rose begins with a spoken joke and then a roll on the toms. Hear how the whole band then comes in at full speed.

genres.name: Riots at the Notting Hill Carnival
genres.text: On 30 August 1976 the Notting Hill Carnival turned into a pitched battle. After an arrest near Portobello Road, Black youths turned on the police, who were present in large numbers. Stones flew and a police van went up in flames. Joe Strummer and Paul Simonon of The Clash became involved. For young Black Londoners it was resistance against intimidating policing.

genres.name: The 100 Club Punk Special
genres.text: On 20 and 21 September 1976 Malcolm McLaren organised a punk festival at the 100 Club on Oxford Street with, among others, the Sex Pistols, The Clash and The Damned. Siouxsie Sioux and Steven Severin stepped in for a band that cancelled. With Sid Vicious on drums they improvised for twenty minutes on the Lord's Prayer. Punk was still a small circle of fans who all knew each other.

genres.name: Sex Pistols: Anarchy in the U.K.
genres.text: Anarchy in the U.K., the first single by the Sex Pistols, came out on 26 November 1976 on EMI. The singer Johnny Rotten sneers that he is an antichrist and an anarchist. The band was formed around the shop SEX of Malcolm McLaren and Vivienne Westwood. Punk sounds simple, but the guitarist Steve Jones recorded his parts several times over each other, creating a wall of guitars.
genres.listen: Notice the beginning: the descending chords, and then Rotten's laugh. Hear how his pronunciation makes every word sharper.

genres.name: Bill Grundy and the Sex Pistols
genres.text: On 1 December 1976 Queen dropped out of the live TV programme Today, and EMI sent the Sex Pistols. Behind the band stood fans from the Bromley Contingent, among them Siouxsie Sioux. The presenter Bill Grundy challenged the band members, and Steve Jones swore heavily at dinner time. The next morning punk was on every front page. Nearly all the concerts of the Anarchy tour were cancelled.

genres.name: The Sex Pistols at Paradiso
genres.text: On 6 and 7 January 1977 the Sex Pistols played at Paradiso, the first punk band in the former church. It was a month after the row around Bill Grundy, and in England they were hardly allowed to play anywhere. The second concert was the last with the bassist Glen Matlock. For young Dutch people in the hall it was the beginning of Dutch punk.

genres.name: The Clash: White Riot
genres.text: Joe Strummer and Paul Simonon of The Clash were there when the Notting Hill Carnival of 1976 turned into riots between Black youths and the police. They wrote White Riot, their first single, which came out in March 1977. Strummer meant it as a call to white young people to stand up for themselves in the same way. He often had to explain that the song was not racist.
genres.listen: The song lasts less than two minutes and begins with a siren. Hear how the band plays as one block, without any rest.

genres.name: Studio 54
genres.text: On 26 April 1977 Steve Rubell and Ian Schrager opened Studio 54 in an old TV studio in Manhattan. At the door Rubell chose himself who was allowed in: celebrities, beautiful people and striking figures. On New Year's Eve 1977 Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards of Chic were turned away. Angry, they wrote a song about it, which later became Le Freak.
genres.listen: Le Freak became the best-selling single in Atlantic's history. Hear how Rodgers's guitar plays small, dry chords above Edwards's bass.

genres.name: God Save the Queen on the Thames
genres.text: God Save the Queen by the Sex Pistols came out on 27 May 1977, in the middle of the celebrations for Queen Elizabeth's silver jubilee. The BBC did not play it and big shops refused to sell it. On 7 June the band played on a boat on the Thames, past Parliament. The police intervened and arrested, among others, the manager Malcolm McLaren. The single reached number 2.
genres.listen: Rotten sings that there is no future. Hear how he repeats the last words over and over until it becomes a chant.

genres.name: Donna Summer: I Feel Love
genres.text: Donna Summer and the producers Giorgio Moroder and Pete Bellotte made I Feel Love in Munich. Apart from the voice and a few drum parts, everything comes from a Moog synthesizer, at a time when disco was usually made with strings. It became a number 1 in England. According to David Bowie, Brian Eno came into the studio in Berlin excited: this was the sound of the future.
genres.listen: Listen to the bass that pulses up and down without stopping. Summer's voice floats on top of it. Do you hear an ordinary guitar or piano?

genres.name: Dutch punk
genres.text: After the Sex Pistols at Paradiso, things went fast. In August 1977 KoeCrand appeared, a fanzine modelled on Sniffin' Glue. Paul Tornado made the first Dutch punk single, Van Agt Casanova, about the politician Dries van Agt. Bands such as Ivy Green, The Ex and the Rondos followed. Dutch punk grew together with the squatters' movement, in squats and little shops such as No Fun on the Rozengracht.
genres.listen: Listen to Van Agt Casanova by Paul Tornado. What does it take over from British punk, and what makes it Dutch?

genres.name: Saturday Night Fever
genres.text: In December 1977 Saturday Night Fever came to the cinemas, based on a report about young Italian Americans in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn. John Travolta plays Tony, who sells paint during the week and on Saturday is the king of the discotheque 2001 Odyssey, in a white suit. The soundtrack with the Bee Gees was number 1 for 24 weeks. Disco became a worldwide fashion, far from the underground clubs.
genres.listen: Stayin' Alive plays under the opening scene in which Tony walks down the street. Hear how the tempo fits a brisk walking pace exactly, with the falsetto voices of the Bee Gees above it.

genres.name: Rock Against Racism in Victoria Park
genres.text: In August 1976 Eric Clapton spoke out at a concert in Birmingham in support of the racist Enoch Powell. The photographer Red Saunders and friends wrote an angry letter to the music press: half of Clapton's music was Black. That is how Rock Against Racism began. On 30 April 1978 tens of thousands of people walked from Trafalgar Square to Victoria Park for a concert with, among others, The Clash, Steel Pulse and X-Ray Spex.
genres.listen: Steel Pulse came from Birmingham, the city of Clapton's remarks. Compare their reggae with the punk of X-Ray Spex: two sounds at one festival against racism.

genres.name: 2 Tone in Coventry
genres.text: On 4 May 1979 Gangsters by The Specials came out, the first record on 2 Tone, the label that the keyboard player Jerry Dammers had started in Coventry. The name stands for Black and white together: the bands were mixed and played ska with the speed of punk. On the B-side was a song by The Selecter, and Madness also began at 2 Tone. Fans wore pork-pie hats again, and black and white checked clothes.
genres.listen: Gangsters is built on Al Capone by the Jamaican ska singer Prince Buster. Compare the tempo with the Jamaican ska of the 1960s: faster, harder and more nervous.

genres.name: Disco Demolition Night
genres.text: On 12 July 1979 you could get into a baseball game in Chicago for 98 cents if you brought a disco record. The radio DJ Steve Dahl blew up the records between two games. More than fifty thousand people came instead of twenty thousand. Thousands stormed the field, set records on fire and destroyed the grass. Many critics saw in the hatred of disco also a hatred of Black and gay music.

genres.name: Sugarhill Gang: Rapper's Delight
genres.text: Sylvia Robinson of Sugar Hill Records in Englewood put three rappers together as the Sugarhill Gang in 1979. Rapper's Delight lasted almost fifteen minutes in the long version, over the bass line of Good Times by Chic. It became the first rap record in the American Top 40. The pioneers from the Bronx thought it was fake, but this was how the world first heard what happened at parties there.
genres.listen: Hear how the rappers rhyme in turn over a groove that never changes. Do you recognise the bass of Good Times?

genres.name: The Coronation Riot
genres.text: On 30 April 1980 Beatrix became queen in the Nieuwe Kerk on the Dam. Squatters, punks, students and football supporters protested against the housing shortage with the slogan no home, no coronation. Around the Dam, the Blauwbrug and the Vondelstraat they fought with thousands of police and military police. Some six hundred people were injured. No future was for many Dutch young people more than a punk slogan.

genres.name: The Specials: Ghost Town
genres.text: Ghost Town by The Specials came out on 12 June 1981. Jerry Dammers wrote it about English cities that were emptying because of unemployment, with closed clubs and young people without a future. In July it was number 1 for three weeks, just when riots broke out in Toxteth, Moss Side and other districts. For many fans it was both the high point and the end of 2 Tone.
genres.listen: The song is in a minor key, with a ghostly organ and horns that recall music from the Middle East. Underneath lies a slow reggae rhythm with the offbeat.
